1.pericope_label: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah this word came unto Jeremiah from the Lord, saying, Take thee a roll of a book, and write therein all the words that I have spoken unto thee against Israel, and against Judah, and against all the nations, from the day I spake unto thee, even unto this day. It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the evil which I purpose to do unto them. Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah

schools.summary: Denies that a collection of the addresses was intended, holding the writing merely a means of presenting their whole contents once more, and fills in the year in which the conqueror took the city and made the king tributary, arguing that the command to write came only towards its end; dates the phrase for a book-roll, which occurs in no earlier prophet or historical book and probably followed the coming in of parchment, and reads the verse as a window into the prophet's workshop, where he speaks unpremeditated, a disciple reports, and the master afterwards collects and revises.

Argues for writing from the fugitive nature of speech, since a hearer takes in only what his capacity allows while what is written can be weighed at leisure and read years after, takes the word for the volume in its blank state and traces the Hebrew and Latin names alike to roots meaning to roll, and holds that God suggested afresh what had slipped the prophet's memory, so that he stood between God and the scribe.

Describes the manufacture of such rolls from copies in hand, vellum or half-tanned sheepskin cut into lengths, stitched, wound on a roller and written in columns, sometimes on two rollers so that the reader coils with one hand what he reads off with the other, and calls the writing a memorial so that the truth of the words might appear when the time came for their fulfilment.

Gives four reasons for the writing at once: that what was only spoken might be reviewed and last longer, that what was delivered at large might be contracted so the parts could be compared, that a second hearing might take hold where the first made no impression, and that single sermons already published might be gathered so none be lost.

debates.question: Why was the spoken word now to be written down?

positions.view: four reasons together: permanence, compression for comparison, a second hearing, and the gathering of scattered sermons into one volume, the writing of Scripture being by divine appointment
because speech is fugitive, a hearer taking in only what his capacity allows before the words glide away, whereas what is written can be weighed at leisure
not to make a collection at all, but merely as the means of presenting the whole contents once more, the prophet being prevented from going himself
as a memorial, so that the truth of the words might appear when the time came for their fulfilment

debates.question: What was a roll of a book?

positions.view: sheets glued together and rolled rather than cut and bound, whence the name volume, still kept for books that are nothing of the kind
vellum or half-tanned sheepskin cut into lengths, stitched and wound on a roller and written in columns, sometimes on two rollers so the reader coils with one hand what he reads off with the other
the word denotes the volume in its blank state, and both the Hebrew and the Latin names derive from roots meaning to roll, as the old archives of Europe still show
a phrase found in no earlier prophet or historical book, which probably followed the coming in of parchment, the roll replacing the papyrus book whose fragile fabric needed another form

debates.question: Why did the prophet not go to the house himself?

positions.view: sacred history records no imprisonment under this king, so a restraint laid on him by God is likelier, and it is not improbable that after his earlier trial he had been forbidden the temple precincts
some hindrance, but probably not imprisonment, since the two men could afterwards hide themselves
simply that he was prevented from getting to the house

outliers.reading: Finds in the command a window into the prophet's workshop: he speaks without premeditation as the word comes to him, a disciple acts as reporter and preserves the utterance, and from time to time the master collects, repeats, revises and edits what he has said; what the chapter records is therefore the history of the first volume of these discourses, which perished, though the book's earlier chapters are substantially a reproduction of it.

Holds that God suggested afresh to the prophet what had slipped from his memory, since the greater part of so many words spoken over so many years must otherwise have escaped him, so that he stood between God and the scribe.

themes: And it came to pass in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, that this word came unto Jeremiah from the Lord, saying,

Take thee a roll of a book, and write therein all the words that I have spoken unto thee against Israel, and against Judah, and against all the nations, from the day I spake unto thee, from the days of Josiah, even unto this day.
It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the evil which I purpose to do unto them; that they may return every man from his evil way; that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin.
Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah: and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the Lord, which he had spoken unto him, upon a roll of a book.

5.pericope_label: And Jeremiah commanded Baruch, saying, I am shut up; I cannot go into the house of the Lord: therefore go thou, and read in the roll, which thou hast written from my mouth, the words of the Lord in the ears of the people in the Lord’s house upon the fasting day. It may be they will present their supplication before the Lord. And in the fifth year of Jehoiakim, in the ninth month, they proclaimed a fast before the Lord

schools.summary: Assigns the fast to the king on hearing that the army was near and supplies a motive that recasts the scene, since it was probably called on the advice of the priests and false prophets to rouse the people to a religious resistance, which would explain the prophet's eagerness to counteract it; prefers the Hebrew year to the Greek, allows some months between the writing and the reading, and adds that the courts would be more than usually thronged and the people more disposed to listen.

Gives the fast to the people rather than the king on the authority of the older versions and the Hebrew, supplies the second reason for choosing that day, since a fast enjoined to deprecate wrath ought to have left the hearers submissive and teachable, notes that the prophet did not shelter behind his scribe but told him to read from the volume, commends the scribe's promptitude in a dangerous and unpopular office, and joins prayer to conversion while denying that pardon rests on repentance rather than on gratuitous mercy.

Calls the fast day a favourable time for such prophecies, since multitudes would be gathered from all parts to implore mercy, and keeps the physical image in the falling of the supplication, men prostrating themselves to deplore their sins.

Gives the fast to the government without deciding which order proclaimed it, supposes the occasion the invading army or a want of rain, allows that the writing may have taken the best part of a year or only a month or two, and thinks the scribe had already read to smaller companies before this most solemn reading of the whole.

debates.question: Who proclaimed the fast, and why?

positions.view: the government, on account of the invading army or a want of rain, though whether king, princes or priests ordered it is not certain
the king, on hearing that the army was near, probably on the advice of the priests and false prophets, to rouse the people to a holy war of religious resistance
the people, since the older versions and the Hebrew make them the subject and so ungodly a king would not have called it
the people cannot have called it, since those from the country towns came up only in consequence of its being appointed; the phrase is probably used generally of keeping a fast

debates.question: Why was that day chosen for the reading?

positions.view: for the concourse, multitudes being gathered from all parts to implore mercy, which made it a favourable time for such prophecies
for the concourse and for the fitness of the day, since a fast enjoined to supplicate mercy and deprecate wrath ought to have left them submissive and teachable
because the courts would be more than usually thronged and the people more than usually disposed to listen

debates.question: How long did the roll lie written before it was read?

positions.view: apparently fourteen months, from the seventh month of the fourth year to the ninth of the fifth, but only two if the month is counted from the spring
the writing may have taken the best part of a year, or only a month or two; the scribe had probably read to smaller companies before this most solemn reading
some months, during which the substance was perhaps made known to the inner circle of the prophet's disciples; the Hebrew year is preferable to the one the Greek gives

outliers.reading: Canvasses the accounts of the prophet's being shut up without settling any: he reports the reading that he was in prison and rejects it, since an order to arrest him afterwards would then have been needless; reports another that the king had confined him to his house; and offers two of his own, a restraint of the Spirit or some legal pollution unfitting him for the courts.

Joins prayer and conversion as both necessary, since a man who seeks reconciliation in words only will not succeed, and then guards the joining, since a sinner might repent a thousand times and remain exposed to judgment: pardon rests not on repentance but on the gratuitous mercy that embraces him.

themes: And Jeremiah commanded Baruch, saying, I am shut up; I cannot go into the house of the Lord:

Therefore go thou, and read in the roll, which thou hast written from my mouth, the words of the Lord in the ears of the people in the Lord’s house upon the fasting day: and also thou shalt read them in the ears of all Judah that come out of their cities.
It may be they will present their supplication before the Lord, and will return every one from his evil way: for great is the anger and the fury that the Lord hath pronounced against this people.
And Baruch the son of Neriah did according to all that Jeremiah the prophet commanded him, reading in the book the words of the Lord in the Lord’s house.

And it came to pass in the fifth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, in the ninth month, that they proclaimed a fast before the Lord to all the people in Jerusalem, and to all the people that came from the cities of Judah unto Jerusalem.

10.pericope_label: Then read Baruch in the book the words of Jeremiah in the house of the Lord, in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the scribe, in the ears of all the people. When Michaiah the son of Gemariah had heard all the words, then he went down into the king’s house, and declared unto the princes all that he had heard. Therefore all the princes sent Jehudi unto Baruch. And they said, Go, hide thee, thou and Jeremiah

schools.summary: Places the chamber and traces its owner's family through three generations of devout patriotism, from the father who worked on the restoration of the house and published the newly found book of the law to the son who now lends his room to the prophet's delegate, explains the messenger's unusually long pedigree from the law of proselyte incorporation, and finds in the princes' alarm a conflict of feeling that left them no alternative but to report what had reached their official knowledge; the tense of the question about the writing is read as continued action, and so as dictation.

Declines to decide why the report was carried down, since the man may have been an informer ingratiating himself as courtiers do or may have been filled with wonder at what he thought incredible, allows the princes' fear was real enough for them to seat the scribe respectfully while marking their turning to one another as the sign that it was not genuine, and calls their care not to offend the king the religion of the court, which fears God just so far as not to lose favour.

Repoints the question about the writing to ask whether the scribe copied the words or wrote them as they were prophesied, has the princes convinced the prophecy was from God and anxious to save both men yet obliged to inform, and draws the consequence the others leave implicit, that without a special influence of God it had been impossible to recall all that was spoken at several times over so many years.

debates.question: Why did the son of Gemariah carry the report down to the palace?

positions.view: good will rather than ill, since he brings no charge and his father afterwards joins those who plead against the burning
not unfriendly, and probably part of a preconcerted plan between the prophet and his friends, the report giving an opening to bring the scribe before the king's counsellors
undecidable: he may have been an informer ingratiating himself as courtiers do, or he may have been filled with wonder and carried up what he thought incredible

debates.question: Why is the messenger's pedigree so unusually long?

positions.view: its two ends explain it: the last name means Ethiopian and belonged to an alien turned proselyte, and since the law admitted such a man's descendants to full incorporation only in the third generation, the name meaning Jew fell naturally to the child who first became entitled to it
two scholars take both names for appellatives rather than proper names on the same ground
he was, on one authority, the king's apparitor

debates.question: What did the princes' fear amount to?

positions.view: a conflict of feelings, alarm for themselves and their country at woes they half believed and alarm for the two men bold enough to utter them, with no hostile purpose but no alternative to reporting what had come to their official knowledge

real enough to seat the scribe respectfully, but not genuine, since the turning of one to another betrays a wavering mind where a man who fears rightly examines himself before God; their care not to offend the king is the religion of the court
enough at least to hear patiently, which the king afterwards would not do
conviction that the prophecy was from God and anxiety to save both men, yet an obligation to inform

outliers.reading: Traces the chamber's owner through a family that furnished three generations of devout patriotism: the father worked with the high priest on the restoration of the house, published the contents of the newly found book of the law and probably ordered copies made; one son protected the prophet; and this son lends his chamber to the prophet's delegate, the gate itself perhaps being part of the father's building work, which would explain a chamber over it falling to him.

Gets the sense of the question about the writing from the tense, which expresses continued action and so means dictation, a thing requiring much time, the circumstantial clause showing that the scribe did nothing else throughout but write.

themes: Then read Baruch in the book the words of Jeremiah in the house of the Lord, in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the scribe, in the higher court, at the entry of the new gate of the Lord’s house, in the ears of all the people.
When Michaiah the son of Gemariah, the son of Shaphan, had heard out of the book all the words of the Lord,

Then he went down into the king’s house, into the scribe’s chamber: and, lo, all the princes sat there, even Elishama the scribe, and Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, and Elnathan the son of Achbor, and Gemariah the son of Shaphan, and Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the princes.
Then Michaiah declared unto them all the words that he had heard, when Baruch read the book in the ears of the people.

Therefore all the princes sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Cushi, unto Baruch, saying, Take in thine hand the roll wherein thou hast read in the ears of the people, and come. So Baruch the son of Neriah took the roll in his hand, and came unto them.
And they said unto him, Sit down now, and read it in our ears. So Baruch read it in their ears.
Now it came to pass, when they had heard all the words, they were afraid both one and other, and said unto Baruch, We will surely tell the king of all these words.
And they asked Baruch, saying, Tell us now, How didst thou write all these words at his mouth?
Then Baruch answered them, He pronounced all these words unto me with his mouth, and I wrote them with ink in the book.
Then said the princes unto Baruch, Go, hide thee, thou and Jeremiah; and let no man know where ye be.

20.pericope_label: And they went in to the king into the court, but they laid up the roll in the chamber of Elishama the scribe. Now the king sat in the winterhouse in the ninth month, and there was a fire on the hearth burning before him. And when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire, until all the roll was consumed. Yet they were not afraid, nor rent their garments

schools.summary: Makes the leaving of the roll an official precaution, so that the document would be available for reference if either man were prosecuted, grants that the English suggests a papyrus book while the Hebrew word will bear either sense, and observes that the Hebrew leaves it as uncertain as the English whether the king cut and burned the roll himself; contrasts an earlier king who rent his garments in a like case and separates the court attendants who felt nothing from the princes who had been alarmed.

Makes the leaving of the roll courtly timidity, since there is no independence at court and the greatest flatterer stands highest, and finds the princes' regard for God small and frigid, for if they believed the roll came from the Spirit the king's displeasure should not have weighed so much; speaks of the burning as one astonished, holding that a simple statement carries more force than invective, since men who grow harder when God fulminates show a diabolical madness and a sign of reprobation.

Describes the winter apartment as suited to a month when snow often lies in that country and the fire as a brazier of coals, the rich burning wood in brass or earthen pans set anywhere in the room while the poor burn sticks on the floor; settles the disputed word for columns, credits the three who interceded with a greater dread of God, and agrees that the search for the two men failed because God did not permit it.

Watches who was made to read the roll, and finds neither the scribe who could have read it with most authority and affection, nor a prince to whom it would have been no disparagement, nor the king himself, but the page then in waiting, who perhaps scarcely knew how to make sense of it: those who despise the word of God so, he adds, soon show that they hate it too.

debates.question: Why did the princes leave the roll behind when they went in to the king?

positions.view: an official precaution, since the document had to be available for reference if either man were prosecuted, and lodging it with the keeper of the archives shows they already feared what the king did
courtly timidity, since there is no independence at court and the greatest flatterer stands highest, so men who would not offend tender ears carried a report rather than the thing itself
mere protocol, since they would first send to learn whether the king could be spoken with

debates.question: Were the three or four things read leaves or columns?

positions.view: either the glued breadths or the columns, though a rabbinic view makes them verses of the Lamentations
columns, since the sacred books are written in them and the word denotes the openings between one and the next
divisions rather than leaves; the inference that the thing was a leaved book cannot be substantiated, since the synagogues still use true rolls wound on a stick with the text divided into parts
the English suggests a papyrus book while the Hebrew word will bear either sense

debates.question: Who was the Jerahmeel sent to make the arrest?

positions.view: the proper name of a servant, since it is not probable the king would send his own son and his eldest could not then have been grown
the king's son in the sense of a member of the royal house, as the Greek rightly renders, the king having been only twenty-five at his accession
a royal prince rather than the king's own son, since the phrase would otherwise have been different

outliers.reading: Watches the choice of reader and makes it the measure of the king's contempt: not the scribe, who could have read the roll with more authority and affection than anyone; not one of the princes, to whom it would have been no disparagement; least of all the king himself; but the page then in waiting, who perhaps scarcely knew how to make sense of what he read.

Speaks of the burning as one astonished and holds that the simple statement carries more force than any invective, since that mortals should not be moved when God fulminates but grow harder is a diabolical madness and a sign of reprobation; and turns the intercession of the three into an aggravation, men drawn back by others and persevering still being the less excusable.

themes: And they went in to the king into the court, but they laid up the roll in the chamber of Elishama the scribe, and told all the words in the ears of the king.

So the king sent Jehudi to fetch the roll: and he took it out of Elishama the scribe’s chamber. And Jehudi read it in the ears of the king, and in the ears of all the princes which stood beside the king.
Now the king sat in the winterhouse in the ninth month: and there was a fire on the hearth burning before him.

And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth.
Yet they were not afraid, nor rent their garments, neither the king, nor any of his servants that heard all these words.
Nevertheless Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the roll: but he would not hear them.
But the king commanded Jerahmeel the son of Hammelech, and Seraiah the son of Azriel, and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel, to take Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet: but the Lord hid them.

27.pericope_label: Then the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, after that the king had burned the roll, saying, Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll. Therefore thus saith the Lord of Jehoiakim king of Judah; He shall have none to sit upon the throne of David; and his dead body shall be cast out in the day to the heat, and in the night to the frost. Then took Jeremiah another roll

schools.summary: Places the fresh command during the concealment and thinks the present form of an earlier chapter is owing to it, reconciles the sentence about the throne with the fact that a son did reign by noting that the boy-prince held a tributary throne three months only and that the next king was a brother rather than a son, and reads the closing verse as showing the genesis of the present volume, the temple discourse revised, enlarged and dictated again.

Observes that God has another way with the rebellious, ceasing to speak and judging in silence, and explains why he took the opposite course here, since the king had supposed a power reduced to ashes extinguished with the parchment; works the Hebrew of the sentence, which says not that none shall sit but that none shall be to him, supplies the reason for the unburied body in the despising of a timely warning, and answers that the second roll went unpunished not by any change in the king but because God bridles the violence he does not soften.

Notes that no duplicate of the first roll had been kept, so the same matter had to be given again with the judgment on the king added, takes the sentence at its hardest as no successor at all and an untimely end without burial, draws the moral that a man who destroys the evidence against him doubles his punishment, and supposes the additions to the second roll were threatenings of temporary importance which the Spirit did not think proper to record.

debates.question: Why was the burned roll written again rather than the matter dropped?

positions.view: because the king had supposed a power reduced to ashes extinguished with the parchment, whereas the word cannot be bound; the renewed threatening came not in hope of benefit but to expose the madness to ridicule
because no duplicate had been kept, so the same matter had to be given again, with the heavy judgment on the king now added
the command falls in the period of concealment, and to it we probably owe the present form of an earlier chapter

debates.question: How can it be said that none should sit upon the throne, when a son did reign?

positions.view: the boy-prince held a tributary throne for three months only, and the king who followed was a brother rather than a son

the Hebrew says not that none shall sit but that none shall be to him, so the exclusion is of his own posterity; the three months went uncounted, and the uncle who followed was set up by the conqueror out of ill-will, to degrade the two he displaced
none who should reign any considerable time
no successor at all, and an untimely end without burial

debates.question: What became of the enlarged roll?

positions.view: it shows the genesis of the present volume, the discourse delivered in the temple court having been revised, enlarged and dictated to the same scribe, and in that shape probably come down to us
the additions were threatenings of temporary importance and local application, which the Spirit did not think proper to record

the point is the constancy of the man who dictated it, who had lately fled in fear and knew the king had ordered him killed, and who went on to exasperate him further, preferring the duty laid on him to his life

outliers.reading: Alone attends to the naming of the king, holding that the title is given not for honour but to show how vainly he gloried in it, since the prophet had been set over nations and kingdoms and sent to reprove mountains and hills, and no elevation in the world could intercept prophetic truth; he reads the clause as encouragement to the prophet as much as sentence on the king, lest a high position terrify the man who had to deliver it.

Ties the punishment to the act itself, the cutting and burning having been done by the king or by his order, with his sons perhaps looking on pleased and his servants assenting, three excepted; and observes that the address is delivered concerning the king rather than to him, the prophet being still in hiding and sought for.

themes: Then the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, after that the king had burned the roll, and the words which Baruch wrote at the mouth of Jeremiah, saying,
Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah hath burned.

And thou shalt say to Jehoiakim king of Judah, Thus saith the Lord; Thou hast burned this roll, saying, Why hast thou written therein, saying, The king of Babylon shall certainly come and destroy this land, and shall cause to cease from thence man and beast?

Therefore thus saith the Lord of Jehoiakim king of Judah; He shall have none to sit upon the throne of David: and his dead body shall be cast out in the day to the heat, and in the night to the frost.

And I will punish him and his seed and his servants for their iniquity; and I will bring upon them, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and upon the men of Judah, all the evil that I have pronounced against them; but they hearkened not.

Then took Jeremiah another roll, and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah; who wrote therein from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire: and there were added besides unto them many like words.
